w: What's tested Carious vs noncarious cervical lesions: the same place on the tooth, a different cause The three causes of NCCLs, alone or together: abrasion (toothbrushing), abfraction (occlusion) and erosion (acid) Abrasion: the toothpaste matters more than the toothbrush; relative dentin abrasivity (RDA); soft brushes, less pressure and the dominant-side clue The evidence that not every NCCL comes from toothbrushing Abfraction: why a load on an inclined plane makes a lesion at the cervical area (compression, tension and the fulcrum), its clues and the night guard Erosion vs caries, where vomiting erodes and why, pH vs buffering capacity, and which drinks are worst Matching the treatment to the cause, and when an NCCL needs a restoration This lecture is Dr. Lawson's, prerecorded for the 11/12 session. He starts with a confession: as a dental student he wouldn't have known the difference between a noncarious cervical lesion (NCCL) and a carious cervical lesion. "I would have just said they're all class fives," without thinking hard about why a patient would need a filling down by the gum. Carious or noncarious? A lot of plaque can sit at the cervical area of a tooth, so caries-mediated lesions form there. They look like caries: soft and brown. They are difficult to restore, sitting under the gums in a patient at risk for caries, and a great option for them is resin-modified glass ionomer. Noncarious cervical lesions are in the same location but have a completely different etiology: they are caused by factors that are not caries. His first slide puts the two side by side: the carious lesion is soft-looking brown tooth structure, while a noncarious one can be brown too but looks hard. NCCLs are multifactorial. There are three causes, and a lesion can come from one of them, two of them or all three: Abrasion Toothbrushing, above all the toothpaste A lower-RDA toothpaste; if it's already low, less pressure, with an electric toothbrush that has a pressure sensor Abfraction Occlusion: loads on the occlusal surface flex the tooth A night guard (occlusal splint) to grind on instead of the teeth Erosion Acid sitting on the teeth A less acidic drink; bicarbonate to raise the mouth's pH; perhaps a water rinse Abrasion: the toothbrush and the toothpaste The evidence that brushing can do it. At a lecture he once heard a researcher, Dzakovich ("I can't pronounce his name"), take the position that all NCCLs are produced by toothbrushing. His study brushed extracted teeth set in artificial gums and recreated the look of an NCCL by brushing near the gum line. It also showed that commercial toothbrushes used without toothpaste did not create NCCLs: the toothpaste matters more than the toothbrush. So when you suspect a patient's lesions come from abrasion, talk with them about the toothpaste they use. Relative dentin abrasivity (RDA) rates how abrasive a toothpaste is: the higher the number, the more abrasive, and the lower the number, the less. Recommend toothpastes with lower numbers. His slide adds that a toothpaste's RDA must be below 250 to get the ADA seal. On his chart, a Colgate whitening toothpaste is about 124, and Crest Pro-Health is always very high. You used to have to look a toothpaste up on a list; now you can ask an AI chatbot, which (live in the recording) gave the same 124 as the chart. The brush and how it's used. Most dentists recommend a soft-bristle toothbrush. The study made the toothpaste look more important than the brush, but soft brushes aren't only about abrasion lesions: they are also for gingival health. "Sometimes I forget that there's the pink parts of the mouth." Oral hygiene has to consider both caries and periodontal health. Technique matters too: tell the patient to brush with less pressure. Pressure is hard to judge, so an electric toothbrush with a pressure sensor, which changes color if you press too hard, helps the patient make sure they aren't pressing too hard (he uses one himself). The dominant-side clue. People push harder on the side of their dominant hand, while on the other side they have to pull. So abrasion that looks worse on the patient's dominant side than on the other side points to the toothbrush. A patient with abrasion lesions on the left side but not the right? Ask, "Are you left-handed?" Those are the patients to coach on brushing more gently, perhaps with an electric toothbrush with a sensor. Not every NCCL comes from toothbrushing Some people say all NCCLs come from toothbrushing. That isn't true, and there is evidence against it: Studies of populations with leprosy, people unable to brush their own teeth, found NCCLs. Archaeological populations had NCCLs in times and places where toothbrushes hadn't been invented yet. Animals get them: his mentor, Dr. Burgess, showed a camel with an NCCL, and a study shows NCCLs in a cat (they don't look quite like the ones in people). NCCLs form where a toothbrush doesn't easily go: on the palate, where people don't usually brush, and even subgingivally, where the bristles can't reach. So some NCCLs are caused by toothbrushing, and the rest need another cause. Abfraction: the occlusion How can a load on the occlusal surface make a lesion on the side of the tooth, at the cervical area? Studies using finite element analysis (FEA), the stress images on his slide, show that loads on the inclined planes of the occlusal surface cause stress at the cervical part of the tooth. In materials science, things are almost always stronger in compression than in tension (being pulled apart). A load the tooth isn't supposed to have, on an inclined plane, pushes the crown to one side. The fulcrum is where the tooth is anchored in the bone. One side of the tooth is compressed; on the other side, tensile forces pull apart the bonds within the tooth structure, and where those tensile stresses are, abfraction lesions can form, just above the fulcrum. His analogy: push on a stop sign. It is anchored in the ground (the fulcrum), the side being stretched is under tension, and that's where the damage can occur. In the tooth, the fulcrum is where it is anchored in the bone, and the NCCL forms just above it. How would you know a lesion is abfraction and not abrasion? "It's hard to know," but look for clues that the patient loads their teeth heavily: exostoses and tori sometimes accompany NCCLs, along with opposing wear facets or other generalized wear that shows the patient is wearing their teeth. What to do: an occlusal splint, a night guard (he apologizes in advance to Dr. Givan if that isn't the right term). This one isn't treating TMD: it is a piece of plastic between the patient's teeth, so they grind a sacrificial piece of plastic instead of their teeth. Any of these lesions can also be restored for esthetic reasons if needed. Dr. Givan's L7 slides add a caution: abfraction is supported by in vitro studies, but clinical documentation has neither validated nor rejected it, so he doesn't count it as a primary mechanism of wear. Both lectures agree that NCCLs are multifactorial. Erosion: acid that isn't caries In a sense all destruction of teeth comes down to acid: a cavity is lactic acid dissolving enamel. But caries is bacteria-mediated demineralization, so it occurs only where plaque stagnates: the cervical areas of the teeth, around orthodontic brackets, the occlusal grooves, and proximally just below the contact point. Erosion happens wherever acidic fluids sit, and it isn't the same as caries. His slide sets the two side by side. Bacteria-induced demineralization (caries): a white spot lesion at the cervical area, white spots after orthodontics, occlusal caries and interproximal caries. Chemical-induced demineralization (erosion): the cusp tips, the lingual of the maxillary anteriors (internal acids, such as vomiting), the incisal edges (with tooth wear) and the buccal surfaces (with toothbrush wear). Cupped-out cusp tips. Why do eroded molars show cupped-out areas where the cusp tips used to be? (A side point, he said, "not totally related to this lecture," but one he always thought was cool.) It's a combination of wear and erosion. The patient wears through the enamel of a cusp tip until a pinpoint of dentin shows: the dentin horn under each cusp. As soon as that dentin is exposed, acid selectively dissolves it, because dentin has a higher critical pH than enamel. Vomiting (bulimia, or anyone who throws up a lot) erodes the lingual of the maxillary teeth, mostly the anterior teeth: the facial surfaces are protected by the lip, and the lingual of the mandibular teeth by the tongue. And when acidic fluids sit at the cervical area of the teeth, they make noncarious cervical lesions. Talking to patients about what they drink The first thing to do about erosion is to talk with patients about the acidic things they eat and drink. A dental school classmate of his measured the pH of a whole range of beverages and ranked them from the lowest pH (the worst) to higher. Don't assume patients know what pH numbers mean: plenty of very smart people don't. Give them reference points (he likens the most acidic end of the chart to battery acid; water is 7) and tell them how acidic some of their drinks are. His chart covers more than soft drinks. Coffee: adding milk makes it less acidic (good news for his cappuccinos), and tea is better than coffee. Sparkling waters: what sets their acidity is the amount of carbonic acid, not the flavor, so the bubblier, more carbonated ones are more acidic. His slide puts it as the brand more than the flavor: brands differ in how much carbonic acid they hold, how bubbly they are. pH vs buffering capacity A newer idea is buffering capacity: how much bicarbonate, and so how much of your saliva, it takes to neutralize a drink. If a drink with a pH of 4 takes a lot of bicarbonate to neutralize, it has a high buffering capacity, and that's bad. If it takes only a little saliva, it has a low buffering capacity, and that's good: it is easier to neutralize after you eat or drink it. pH and buffering capacity sound as if they should be the same thing, but they aren't, and they are measured differently. You measure pH by putting a pH probe in the solution. You measure buffering capacity by adding bicarbonate a little at a time and measuring how much it takes to bring the pH back toward neutral (in their experiment, to a pH of 6.5). A dental student in their lab (later a resident, now an endodontist) measured both for a whole range of beverages. Ranked by buffering capacity, the drinks stayed in about the same order as by pH, with two exceptions: orange juice and wine became "way, way bad." On his slide their pH is about 3.6 and 4.0, not the lowest on the chart (the most acidic drink is 2.5), yet they took the most bicarbonate to neutralize. People drink orange juice all the time, so for a patient with a lot of erosion, ask about citrus drinks. Citric acid is a chelator: it wraps around calcium, so citrus drinks and citrus fruit can be extremely erosive to enamel. Telling a patient with erosion to drink only water and milk may make them "lose the will to live," so give them something good that isn't bad for their teeth: Milo's tea. His slide says the unsweet tea; in the recording it's the sweet tea, which, made with Splenda, has no fermentable sugar either. Raising the pH He measured the pH of many mouth rinses too ("kind of a waste of time"): some are low (as low as about 3.2 on his slide), but you rinse for about 30 seconds, maybe twice a day, so it's probably not a big deal. For a patient with a lot of erosion, you can raise the mouth's pH with a base: bicarbonate. Basic Bites are candies that contain bicarbonate and arginine, a prebiotic, and they can help raise the pH of the mouth (he brought them up as an aside, and they are back in his summary). A patient can also rinse with baking soda, which is bicarbonate. Some advice makes sense but, as far as he knows, has no evidence behind it ("kind of wives' tales"): Keep acidic drinks to mealtimes (maybe the cheese on your hamburger helps neutralize your Coca-Cola). Drink through a straw (he teases a colleague who sends his Diet Coke straight past his teeth). Rinse with water after drinking soda or juice. Why water may help less than he'd like: pH is on a logarithmic scale. In the lab, doubling an acid with water doesn't meaningfully change its pH; you'd need "a swimming pool of water." To neutralize an acid before pouring it down the sink, you add a base, such as bicarbonate. Water is fine, just probably not as effective as he wishes. Checking the mouth's pH with pH strips isn't easy either: his own saliva always reads about neutral. Match the treatment to the cause There is value in figuring out the etiology of an NCCL, because then you can treat the cause. If all of a patient's lesions come from sucking on lemons all day, there's little point in talking about the RDA of their toothpaste. To keep the lesions from getting bigger: Toothbrushing: switch to a lower-RDA toothpaste. If it's already low, the patient may be pressing too hard: an electric toothbrush with a pressure sensor. Acid: switch to a less acidic drink; rinse with water after meals (he doesn't know of evidence for it); bicarbonate, such as Basic Bites. Abfraction: a night guard. His slide calls this "what I tell patients," since "who really knows what causes NCCLs": if they don't hurt, look ugly or come near the pulp, he doesn't need to fill them; try to stop them from getting bigger; switch toothpaste; an electric toothbrush with a sensor; more Milo's unsweet tea; rinse with water after meals and acidic foods; and a night guard, with a question mark. The slide's ways to cut acidity (non-water drinks only at mealtimes, a straw, a water rinse after soda or juice) have only anecdotal evidence. When to restore an NCCL What he learned in dental school (not official, he says): you don't necessarily need to restore an NCCL if it is cleansable, doesn't hurt, doesn't look bad and isn't so deep that it is getting close to the pulp. A lesion that can't be cleaned, hurts, looks bad or is deep is the one to restore. The same idea as Dr. Givan's L7 slides, which restore NCCLs only when it becomes necessary (progression, sensitivity, poor esthetics, food collection). Find the cause, treat it, and restore when a lesion is a problem.
